accuracy.evidence: Checked against the AQA GCSE Physics specification 8463 section 4.1.1.3 (specific heat capacity definition and ΔE = m c Δθ, on the equation sheet), the National Curriculum in England KS3 physics (energy changes and heating), NGSS MS-PS3-4, and data tables in the Engineering ToolBox and CRC Handbook: water 4180–4200, ethanol about 2440, vegetable oil about 2000, aluminium 897–900, dry sand about 830, iron 450, copper 385, liquid ammonia about 4700, hydrogen gas cp about 14 300 J/kg K. Every number in the lab and items was recomputed: 42 000 J gives +10, +21 and +52.5 °C; 2 × 4200 × 50 = 420 000 J; 0.5 × 900 × 40 = 18 000 J; 8400 ÷ (0.2 × 4200) = 10 °C; 9000 ÷ (2 × 450) = 10 °C. The adult text states that sea mixing and evaporation also moderate coastal climate and that the beach graph is a sketch, not data.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: a high c means heating quickly (step 1 prediction water vs sand, challenge Q1 and Q4 'water has a low c', p4 distractor), using the final temperature instead of the change (step 4 '588 000 J', challenge '126 000 J', m4), leaving out or misusing the mass (step 4 '210 000 J', '36 000 J', '72 000 J', '2 °C', challenge Q3, m8 grams vs kilograms), dividing the wrong way (0.4 °C, 0.1 °C), confusing c with conductivity (step 2 prediction copper vs aluminium, m6), and explaining the sea by the sun alone (challenge 'the sea is deeper, so it gets more sun').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagspheat drives three thermometers from one energy slider using real c values, makes the learner dial energy into a 1 kg aluminium then copper block until the rise reads exactly 1.00 °C (measuring c by its definition), scales a water mass against an energy bar to hit 84 000 J and 21 000 J, offers ΔE = mcΔθ answers whose distractors are computed slips, and plots sand and sea temperatures through a draggable 24-hour beach day. The heating-curve lab flagheatc plots one sample through changes of state with latent heat; it has no comparison of substances, no c measurement and no mass scaling, and lab_distinct stayed under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers before being told: the trio shows sand at 72.5 °C and water at 30 °C for the same 42 000 J, and the feedback names the rule 'Lower c, bigger rise'; overshooting the 1 °C target says 'Too much: 1.11 °C. Bring it back to exactly 1.00 °C', and hitting it says '900 J warms 1 kg of aluminium by 1 °C, so c = 900 J/kg °C'; the mass bar shows 'Double the mass, double the energy'; wrong sums say '588 000 J used 70 °C, the final temperature, not the 50 °C change'; and the beach graph shows the sand at 11 °C and the sea at 17 °C at 02:00.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options: water and sand warm the same with the same energy (the thermometers disprove it), copper needs more energy per degree because it is a metal that conducts well (the 1 °C measurement gives 385 vs 900), double the mass needs the same energy (the energy bar doubles), and at 2 am the sand is warmer because it was hotter all day (the graph shows it below the sea).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six questions with tagged wrong answers and messages naming the slip: 'a higher c means more energy per degree, so it warms less, not more', '126 000 J uses the final 30 °C. Use the change', '4 200 J is the energy for 1 °C. Multiply by the 10 °C change too', 'does not multiply by the mass properly', 'c is joules per kilogram per degree', and '0.1 °C divides the wrong way round. Δθ = ΔE ÷ (m × c) = 9000 ÷ 900'.

readability.evidence: validate_lessons passes the kid (≤ 6.5) and adult limits after the adult text was split into shorter sentences (it first read at grade 11). Kid paragraphs use a spoon in tea and the beach, give one number pair (4200 vs 800) and one worked change (20 °C to 70 °C is 50 °C). Symbols are introduced once in words: energy = m × c × Δθ.

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matches. Each step has one job (compare substances, measure c, scale with mass, calculate, apply to a coast) and each item explanation shows the working or names the property, for example 'ΔE = 0.5 × 450 × 10 = 2250 J, not 2 250 000 J'.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px (touch, 1.5x) in light and dark for every step before and after Show me: the slider sits at the top with its label, three thermometers fit side by side with readings and c values below, the six energy buttons wrap into two rows, the beach graph keeps its axis labels and both temperature read-outs above the feedback box, and answer tiles are full width.

accessibility.evidence: Every control has a button: ±6 000 J, ±5/10/100 J with labels such as 'Add 100 joules', ±0.5 kg, each answer tile and ±2 hours. The canvas aria-label reads the energy, mass or time and all temperatures after every change, the slider can be dragged anywhere across the top band, challenge feedback is an aria-live status, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.

sources: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification 4.1.1.3 and Physics equation sheet
National Curriculum in England: Key Stage 3 science, physics (energy, changes and heating) (DfE 2013)
The Engineering ToolBox and CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics: specific heat capacities of water, ethanol, vegetable oil, aluminium, sand, iron, copper, ammonia and hydrogen
Met Office: why coastal areas have milder temperatures (sea breezes and the sea's slow warming and cooling)
